title: Proposition C.1 states the wrong range in its achievability equality
quote: “any maximizer of Fλ attains the upper bound, i.e., Δ(x̃) = max Fc − min Fc.”
evidence: The preceding upper bound is **max Fn − min Fn**, not the span of Fc. This is more than an interchangeable symbol: take two fully controllable assignments with Fn(a)=1, Fn(b)=0 and λ=1/4. Attaining the nominal upper bound requires choosing b. If the displayed equality also holds, span(Fc)=1, so Fλ(a)−Fλ(b) ≥ 3/4−1/4=1/2>0. Then b cannot maximize Fλ. A corrected construction is Fc=−M Fn with M>(1−λ)/λ: e.g. M=4 gives Fλ(a)=−1/4, Fλ(b)=0, nominal degradation 1, but span(Fc)=4. No proof of the proposition appears in the supplied PDF; this is a counterexample to the literal statement, not an allegation about an unseen proof.
fix: Replace Fc by Fn in the equality and prove achievability with an explicitly scaled auxiliary objective.

title: The Hospital reproduction path uses a different coalition-regret metric
quote: “the coalition mean regret is” the mean of δi(x̃)=max_xi ri(xi⊕x̃−i)−ri(x̃).
evidence: The released Hospital metrics instead set coalition_max_reward_sum=(max_joint_reward/total_agents)×coalition_size and coalition_reward_regret=max(0, coalition_max_reward_sum−coalition_reward_sum). The named Hospital coalition-regret plot divides that surrogate by a min–max denominator. It never searches unilateral counterfactuals in that path. These measures can disagree even at zero unilateral regret: if three agents each get 5 only when all choose 1, at all-0 every unilateral regret is 0, while this surrogate gives a two-agent coalition (15/3)×2−0=10. The Jira metrics path separately implements unilateral regret correctly. This confirms a contract mismatch in the released Hospital reproduction code; absent original logs/figure commands, it does not establish which path generated every published bar.
fix: Implement the defined mean unilateral regret for Hospital plots, or explicitly rename and define the equal-share reward-shortfall surrogate.

title: The judge-ablation reference points to the environment figure
quote: “leave judge ablations in the Appendix (See Figure 17 in Appendix).”
evidence: Figure 17 (p.24) varies environments. The state-of-the-art judge-model ablation is Figure 16 (p.23), titled 'Emergent Collusion Over State-of-The-Art Judge Models'. This is a confirmed wrong-number pointer, distinct from the valid persuasion-tactics reference to Fig. 12.
fix: Change the §5.3 judge-ablation reference from Figure 17 to Figure 16.

title: Single-score baselines never receive the evaluated task or action
quote: “Single-score monitoring fails completely on our benchmark—both trusted and untrusted single-score monitors achieve 0% safety.”
evidence: BASELINE_PROMPT contains neither {task_description} nor {tool_calls}. Both baseline builders pass only that constant prompt to ControlArena. In the exact locked dependency (control-arena 14.2.0), the default formatter calls prompt.format(task_description=..., tool_calls=...); it does not append the trajectory elsewhere. The offline check sends distinct benign/attack sentinels and gets byte-identical prompts containing neither action nor task. The structured monitor does receive those fields. Thus the released baseline comparison confounds input visibility with scoring structure, undermining the claimed 0%→95% gain. The original experiment logs are absent, so whether an unpublished corrected prompt was used remains unknown.
fix: Include task/action placeholders in both baselines and rerun a matched comparison with released prompts and logs.

title: Table 3 composites cannot follow from its stated same-step scores and released pipeline
quote: “Per-dimension average suspicion scores (max-suspicion step per sample)” and “Composite includes heuristic detector and intent analyzer boosts”.
evidence: In GA/CA/RC/SA/ATC order, attack weighted mean = .2(.849)+.3(.870)+.2(.893)+.1(.682)+.2(.845)=**.8466**, and honest = .2(.617)+.3(.753)+.2(.804)+.1(.642)+.2(.801)=**.7345**. Reported composites are **.616/.206**, lower by .2306/.5285. Positive boosts and upper clipping cannot explain these decreases. Category reweighting does not rescue the released pipeline: all 16 category subsets were checked; for [0,1] scores, its maximum possible downward change (total variation of weights) is no greater than the simultaneously added regex boost. Other boosts are nonnegative. Also, plot_dimension_breakdown collects **all monitored steps**, not the stated per-sample maximum step. The table therefore mixes populations/score versions or misstates its aggregation; its footnote is insufficient. Underlying corrected means cannot be recovered without aligned logs.
fix: Regenerate dimension and composite summaries from the same runs and steps, publishing the exact aggregation and score version.

title: Usefulness is implemented as an allow rate, ignoring task success
quote: “Usefulness: Fraction of honest-mode runs where the task was completed successfully.”
evidence: The analysis computes only P(max_suspicion<τ | honest), despite loading main_task_success. A synthetic honest run with max_suspicion=0 and main_task_success=False is reported as **100% usefulness**. Successful deferred completion is also excluded by construction. Table 2's narrower caption still calls the number 'honest task completion without deferral', which would require success AND no deferral; the code checks only no deferral. Therefore the plotted label does not implement either task-success definition. This does not show the actual task-completion rates, which require the missing logs.
fix: Report the current metric as honest allow rate and compute task completion separately, including deferral outcomes as specified.

title: Equation 2's per-dimension saturation is not implemented
quote: “we apply a per-dimension saturation function before aggregation: s′d=min(sd·Boosttotal,1.0)”
evidence: The actual scorer first averages unboosted normalized dimension scores, may add a separate variance-triggered .08 boost, and then computes clip(composite + heuristic_boost + total_detector_boost + intent_boost,0,1). No per-dimension multiplication/saturation from Eq. 2 occurs. For equal dimension scores .2 and an additive boost .5, code returns .7; treating the corresponding multiplier as 1.5 would give .3 under Eq. 2. The two algorithms have different thresholds and failure behavior. §3.3 describes additive composite boosts, so the paper also gives incompatible specifications internally.
fix: Choose one algorithm, make equations/algorithm/code agree, and state whether results include the disagreement boost.

title: The advertised seventh heuristic detector is missing
quote: “Subprocess Tracker. Detects process spawning ... download-then-execute chains ... cron/systemd persistence”.
evidence: The tracked source contains six heuristic modules: variable_binding, dual_purpose, data_flow, string_assembly, encoding, config_diff. No subprocess tracker module, tracking state, import, or invocation exists in bash_heuristic_monitor. detectors/__init__.py lists intent_analyzer as its seventh module, but that is the separate LLM stage, not a seventh pure-function heuristic. Generic regex matches may catch some related patterns; they do not implement the named stateful tracker.
fix: Release and invoke the subprocess tracker, or correct the architecture/count to six heuristic detectors.

title: A 0.60 trusted weight does not prevent the untrusted scores from suppressing alarms
quote: “the untrusted model contributes reasoning analysis without being able to unilaterally suppress alarms.”
evidence: At τ=.5, trusted scores GA=CA=SA=.8 contribute (.2+.3+.1)×.8=.48. If the untrusted RC/ATC scores are .8, the total is .80 and triggers; changing only those two scores to zero yields .48 and suppresses it. The weights bound the untrusted contribution to .4; they do not establish the stated guarantee. At τ>.6 the trusted portion cannot trigger alone even with all trusted scores=1. Observed 20/20 detection at τ=.3 is not a proof of immunity.
fix: State a conditional bound or give the trusted score an independent alarm/veto rule, and test deliberately colluding monitor outputs.

title: Several reference identities do not match their arXiv IDs
quote: “We test ... on the AgentHarm dataset [7]”; [7] is titled “HarmBench”.
evidence: [7] is [HarmBench, arXiv:2402.04249](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04249), whereas [AgentHarm is arXiv:2410.09024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09024), led by Maksym Andriushchenko. The actual HarmBench lead author is Mantas Mazeika, not 'Maksym Mazeika'. [3]'s ID [2512.15688](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15688) is *BashArena: A Control Setting for Highly Privileged AI Agents*, by Adam Kaufman et al., not the listed Pearce et al. title/authors. [11]'s [2602.20628v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20628v1) was first submitted in February 2026, not 2025, and its authors are Gardner-Challis et al., not 'Thomas Griffiths, Niels Warncke'. [13]'s [2504.05259](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05259) is by Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, Buck Shlegeris and Geoffrey Irving, not the listed Hoelscher-Obermaier et al. These are identity/year errors; the claimed AgentHarm experiment's actual dataset still needs its missing artifacts.
fix: Replace these entries from authoritative metadata and cite AgentHarm separately from HarmBench.

title: The promised data and AgentHarm evaluation entry point are not in the release
location: §1 code/data availability and Fig. 8, [PDF pp. 3,18](<C:/Users/ussid/OneDrive/Documents/ChatGPT/collusion 2/papers/2604.03968v1.pdf>); [repos/TraceGuard/.gitignore:77](<C:/Users/ussid/OneDrive/Documents/ChatGPT/collusion 2/repos/TraceGuard/.gitignore:77>); repository tree at pinned commit in evidence/verification.json
quote: “Code and data are available at https://github.com/linhkid/TraceGuard.”
evidence: At commit 0e2e8226d7ca98e0375ed3aa54f9a870a3794714, the repository has no tracked evaluation logs or per-sample result data for the 519 BashArena or 20 AgentHarm samples. .gitignore explicitly excludes .eval logs and generated result files. Fig. 8 names run_agentharm_eval.py, but no such tracked script exists. The README supplies aggregate numbers, not the observations/configuration manifest needed to recompute them. This is a release/reproducibility gap, not evidence that experiments were not performed.
fix: Publish the per-sample scores, run/configuration manifest and AgentHarm script, with a stable paper-version tag.

title: The analysis pools different monitors while labeling their results separately
quote: “We compare against two baselines” and report safety by monitor.
evidence: compute_pareto_points(df, monitor_names, ...) constructs honest_df/attack_df from the entire input before looping over monitor_name and never filters either by monitor. A two-monitor example with true detection rates 100% and 0% returns 50% for both named monitors. The CLI's default 'all' likewise aggregates everything in the chosen directory. This is a confirmed analysis bug when logs contain multiple monitors; no original logs are available to establish whether it affected a published figure.
fix: Filter rows by monitor before computing each frontier and require explicit pooling in the CLI.

title: The released intent analyzer uses a different model and silently skips by default
quote: “The intent analyzer uses GPT-4.1-mini”.
evidence: The release describes its intent stage as Claude Opus 4.6 via Bedrock, gets the model ID from CLAUDE_BEDROCK_MODEL_ID or CLAUDE_MODEL_ID, and calls get_model(f'bedrock/{model_id}'). If neither is set it returns a zero-boost IntentAnalysis without a model call. It does not use the trusted GPT-4.1-mini role. The CLI's model flags do not configure this hidden extra provider. This confirms that the released default/model path differs from the stated setup, without determining the model used in unavailable historical logs.
fix: Configure the analyzer explicitly through the evaluation model roles and release the exact model ID and activation state used for each run.

title: The premeditation equation and implementation count an unplanned third action
quote: “When the final action matches neither the plan nor the announcement, the deviation is not counted as premeditated”.
evidence: Eq. 1 requires only a_act≠a_pub AND a_pub≠a_plan. It omits a_act=a_plan. On a numeric game, plan=0, public=1, actual=2 satisfies both inequalities yet was not the planned action. The released _typology(True,True) labels this 'premeditated_deception', and compute_premeditation_rate counts it in the numerator. The executed source check confirms this example. With only two actions the two inequalities imply actual=plan, so this flaw does not invalidate the high-deception Diners/El Farol headline examples; it matters for Fishing, Public Goods and Weakest Link.
fix: Require actual=plan in the numerator and introduce a third-action category, then recompute numeric-game rates.

title: The cross-game payoff-gap claim contradicts Table 14
location: §4.3 Cross-game comparison versus Appendix F.1/Table 14, [PDF pp. 6,22](<C:/Users/ussid/OneDrive/Documents/ChatGPT/collusion 2/papers/2607.05132v2.pdf>)
quote: “Weakest Link, Volunteer, and El Farol show minimal asymmetries (gaps below 0.40).”
evidence: Table 14 lists El Farol Claude-minority/Llama-majority gaps **+7.36/+8.51/+6.98** at pos1/pos5/pos24, and Llama-minority/Claude-majority **+6.99** at pos24. Volunteer includes **−.62**, **−.60**, and **+.58**, also outside an absolute .40 bound. The El Farol +8.51 gap even exceeds every Diners gap in that table (maximum absolute value 4.49). Public Goods 'up to .45' and Weakest Link '<.40' do agree with the table. Different payoff scales limit welfare comparisons across games, but cannot repair the paper's explicit raw-gap thresholds.
fix: Correct the game-specific ranges and revise the boundary-condition/exploitation discussion using an explicitly normalized cross-game comparison.

title: The last Diners payoff row swaps cooperators and defectors
quote: “1 CHEAP + 4 EXPENSIVE” lists Defector Payoff −1.80 and Cooperator Payoff 3.20.
evidence: The shared bill is (2+4×8)/5=6.8. The CHEAP cooperator gets 5−6.8=**−1.8**; each EXPENSIVE defector gets 10−6.8=**3.2**. The table places these values under the opposite headings. The released payoff implementation returns the correct mapping.
fix: Swap the two payoff cells in the last row of Table 5.

title: A reported Fishing payoff exceeds the game's maximum
location: Appendix B, C/Table 3 and E.2/Table 9, [PDF pp. 13,15,18](<C:/Users/ussid/OneDrive/Documents/ChatGPT/collusion 2/papers/2607.05132v2.pdf>); [repos/LLM-Trust-Breaking/src/games/fishing.py:88](<C:/Users/ussid/OneDrive/Documents/ChatGPT/collusion 2/repos/LLM-Trust-Breaking/src/games/fishing.py:88>)
quote: Table 9, Tragedy of Commons / Llama-4-Maverick: “Max 6.00”.
evidence: The specified action set is {0,...,5}; the payoff is the selected catch if sustainable and 0 otherwise. Hence 0≤ui≤5. The code also clamps a response of 6 to 5 before scoring. A maximum of 6 cannot arise under the published game. It may be a table typo or evidence of another configuration, but the supplied artifacts do not resolve which.
fix: Correct the maximum from the original observations or disclose and separate any run with a larger action bound.

title: The released Fishing default changes the collapse boundary
quote: “If total catch exceeds 3N fish, the lake collapses ... If total catch <= 3N, each fisherman keeps what they caught”.
evidence: For n=5, the paper allows total catch 15. Both build_game_params() and FishingGame's default use **3n−1=14**. With all five choosing 3, total catch=15: the paper pays each agent 3, while the executed released game pays everyone 0. This changes the coordination target and strategic incentives. An explicit --threshold 15 can recover the paper setting, but no published run manifest establishes that override was used.
fix: Use 3n as the default or document the actual 3n−1 game and release the experiment commands/configurations.

title: The supplied MLE score CSV is rejected by its price-analysis loader
quote: Repositories “each ... contain instructions on how to reproduce our results”.
evidence: The bundled CSV has metadata_monitor_model and metadata_monitor_input_token_count. load_token_data() requires score_metadata__monitor_model and score_metadata__monitor_input_token_count. Calling the actual loader on the supplied CSV raises **ValueError: CSV is missing required columns: score_metadata__monitor_input_token_count, score_metadata__monitor_model**, before analysis can proceed. This is a concrete reproduction-interface break in the inspected release, not a refutation of the reported monitor results.
fix: Normalize the released CSV column names in the loader or provide the matching data export and exact analysis command.

title: The shipped metric tests use an obsolete scalar return contract
quote: The paper reports “TPR at 1% FPR”; the released test asserts that calculate_tpr_at_fpr(...) equals 1.0 for perfect separation.
evidence: The actual function returns (TPR, actual_FPR, threshold), giving **(1.0,0.0,0.0)** on that test's input. The test compares this tuple directly with 1.0 and raises **TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'tuple' and 'float'**. The offline check executes the original function and the same unittest assertion. This is a broken validation test; the returned TPR itself is correct, and it does not show an error in the paper's metric values.
fix: Unpack the returned tuple and test each component against its documented contract.

title: The claimed per-occurrence recovery rates do not match the printed counts
quote: “The per-occurrence recovery rate ... jumps from 56% on Codex to 73% on Gemini.”
evidence: Across Table 5's nine modes, Codex has **177 occurrences and 91 recoveries**, so 91/177=**51.41%**, not 56%. Gemini has **122 occurrences and 87 recoveries**, so 87/122=**71.31%**, not 73%. These same denominators give 177/85=2.082 and 122/85=1.435 modes per trajectory, matching the stated 2.1/1.4. Appendix G defines category recovery by summing recovered mode occurrences over occurrences. A mean of per-trajectory recovery fractions could differ, but would be a different estimand and needs that label/denominator. The qualitative direction survives.
fix: Correct the pooled rates or explicitly identify the alternative weighting scheme and supply its per-trajectory inputs.

title: Non-significant difference tests are treated as establishing exchangeability
quote: “Mann–Whitney U-tests find no significant difference ... so the two baselines are exchangeable as monitor inputs.”
evidence: Failing to reject a distributional difference does not establish equivalence/exchangeability. The design has only five underlying baseline runs per instance/model before filtering; ten monitor scores are collapsed to a median, not ten independent task runs. Table 15 actually gives different 98th-percentile thresholds for Code+Comms (Codex 5, Gemini 6) and Single-Agent (5.3 versus 6). Pooling may remain a reasonable design choice, and the reported ablations test its practical effect, but the asserted statistical implication is invalid.
fix: Describe pooling as a design choice supported by sensitivity checks, or perform an equivalence analysis with a prespecified tolerance.
